extracted.intended_audience: readers of The Spectator; early-18th-century literate public interested in morals, manners, and essays
extracted.subtask_description: Annotated moral and social essays from The Spectator (early 18th century) offering prescriptive advice on cheerfulness, modesty, prayer, and public behaviour. Includes poetic translations and satirical fables used to illustrate moral points.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cheerfulness as a moral habit and promoter of health
rubrics_metrics.description: Chearfulness is, in the first place, the best Promoter of Health. Repinings and secret Murmurs of Heart give imperceptible Strokes to those delicate Fibres ... Health and Chearfulness mutually beget each other.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cheerfulness banishes anxious care and discontent, soothes and composes the Passions, and keeps the Soul in a perpetual calm. Cultivate cheerfulness by considering the world in its agreeable lights: enjoy the Sun, colours (green in particular), the music and appearance of living creatures, fountains, lakes, rivers, and the variety of day/night and seasons. Recognize that Nature provides both use and delight (flowers, blossoms, landscape) and that indulging in such agreeable sensations supports bodily and mental health. ‘Fence against the Temper of his Climate or Constitution’ by frequently indulging in considerations that give serenity of mind.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mitigate melancholy by attending to accessible pleasures
rubrics_metrics.description: The World is filled with innumerable Objects that are proper to raise and keep alive this happy Temper of Mind; persons of all ranks may find incitements to Chearfulness in Nature and everyday entertainments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If subject to a melancholy climate or constitution (the essay notes 'an Easterly Wind' as an emblem), actively seek and reflect on the agreeable aspects of the world — wild rocks, grotesque parts of nature, works of art, friendship, books, conversation — rather than indulging in repining or secret murmurs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Modesty defined as consciousness of no ill (not mere blushing)
rubrics_metrics.description: Modesty consists in being conscious of no Ill, and not in being ashamed of having done it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A blushing aspect may signal either innocence or guilt; true modesty is an inner state of innocence and confidence. Young women should cultivate confidence and avoid acts that 'ought to stain her Cheeks' so that modesty arises from innocence rather than from timorous affectation (example: Orbicilla is kind but blushing — she has lost the sense of innocence).

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid the occasion of ill to preserve reputation
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘The best ... advice: Is to avoid th' Occasion of the Ill; For when the Cause, whence Evil doth arise, Removed is, th' Effect surceaseth still.’ (Spencer quoted)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical rules recommended especially to young women under the distress of defamation: abstain from pleasure, restrain your will, subdue desire, bridle loose delight, use scanted diet and forbear fill, shun secrecy and talk in open sight. In short: remove temptations and suspicious occasions rather than rely solely on defenders of honour; consistent decent behaviour is the surest guard against calumny.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be aware of social definitions of virtue (appearance vs truth)
rubrics_metrics.description: Public judgement often equates lack of obvious vice with virtue: 'the Crowd ... terms every Woman who will not be a Wench, Virtuous.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that popular labels ('virtuous', 'man of honour') are sometimes applied on the basis of minimal outward signs; maintain a genuine habit of decency rather than relying on social shorthand. The essay satirizes the lax standards by which people self-apply and accept moral labels.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use set forms of prayer to restrain folly and extravagant petitions
rubrics_metrics.description: By set forms of Prayer the Folly and Extravagance of Mens Desires may be kept within due Bounds, and not break out in absurd and ridiculous Petitions on so great and solemn an Occasion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Menippus fable (voices of prayers heard by Jupiter) illustrates the vanity and inconsistency of many private petitions (riches, revenge, petty requests). The essay endorses set forms as a way to keep petitions serious and reasonable, preventing absurd or self-serving prayers from dominating religious practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dealing with atheists and irreligion (recommended public stance)
rubrics_metrics.description: Atheists who depreciate Religion and strip Mankind of useful social practices should be treated with scorn and mockery rather than reasoned with at length; retort their own weapons upon them, using scorn and mockery.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author argues that atheists gain undeserved prominence by being argued with; ridicule and contempt undercuts their pretensions. At the same time, those with particular schemes of worship should be treated with tenderness and corrected with temper and humanity. A caution is given: excessive zeal may misdirect and harm (e.g., could turn to persecuting sectaries).

rubrics_metrics.name: Caveat about zeal: avoid excessive persecution in enforcing religious or moral norms
rubrics_metrics.description: Zeal for Religion is of so active a Nature, that it seldom knows where to rest; after having discharged our Atheists, we might possibly think of shooting off our Sectaries.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even while advocating strong public responses to atheism (mockery) the essay warns against measures that go too far — zeal can escalate to persecuting others and ultimately become dangerous to dissenters and possibly oneself. Exercise moderation.
